Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken shakes hands with then-AIPAC President Michael Tuchin before delivering remarks at the AIPAC Policy Summit in Washington, DC, on June 5, 2023 [File: Jess Rapfogel/AP Photo]By Umar FarooqPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Nearly a year before he stunned many by winning a seat in the United States Senate from Texas, James Talarico drew attention for his vehement rejection of campaign funding from the country’s largest pro-Israel lobbying group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
“I’ve never taken money from AIPAC, and I’m not taking money from AIPAC in this campaign,” Talarico said in a clip for a podcast that later went viral. “Seeing what’s happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being.”
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Jamaal Bowman: ‘If I had kept my mouth shut, I’d be in Congress’list 2 of 3Why did Democrat Haley Stevens just endorse a Republican for US Senate?list 3 of 3Could the US midterms further isolate Israel in Washington?end of list
On November 3, Talarico won by more than 12 percentage points. Pro-Israel groups allied with AIPAC gave modest support – about $6,000 – to Talarico’s opponent, Ken Paxton, but Talarico’s willingness to be so open about his disdain for AIPAC is still a notable part of a shift in US politics.
In races across the country, AIPAC and political spending groups linked to it poured tens of millions of dollars into backing one candidate or another. While the group did back many winning candidates, nearly two-thirds of the total money it spent this election cycle went to those who ended up losing.

A police car is parked in front of the house of Malaysia's former Prime Minister Najib Razak in Kuala Lumpur on November 4, 2026 [AFP]By AFP and ReutersPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Malaysia’s king has warned that any attempt to challenge his order granting jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak house arrest could amount to defying ⁠his decree, a day after authorities delayed Najib’s transfer.
The 73-year-old Najib was jailed for his role in one of the largest-ever global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund, the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Malaysia’s ex-PM Najib found guilty of money laundering, abuse of powerlist 2 of 3Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justicelist 3 of 3Malaysian ex-PM Najib’s bid to serve prison term at home delayedend of list
But King Sultan Ibrahim granted him a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to serve out the rest of his sentence at home provided he paid a $12m fine.
On Friday, the country’s attorney general blocked the former prime minister’s transfer to house arrest after the fine was paid, saying his office needed more clarification on the pardon.
The king said on Saturday there was nothing to clarify, calling the pardon “clear, evident and without any ambiguity”.
“There should be no confusion in interpretation,” King Ibrahim said in a statement, adding it was not tied to any other cases against the former leader.
“Given that all conditions in the conditional pardon order have been fulfilled, any argument questioning the order leads towards denying the order of His Majesty the King.”

A Yemeni government fighter fires a mortar on the front lines of Yemen's war [Handout: Yemeni Army]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Yemeni government forces say they have repelled Houthi assaults in Marib, as the armed group said strikes on a village in Sanaa province had killed at least 27 people.
In a statement on Saturday, government forces said troops backed by warplanes and drones had fought for hours to halt Houthi advances in Marib province, destroying fortifications and combat equipment.

It said troops were also pushing into Houthi-held areas of al-Jawf province, where fighting entered a third consecutive day as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation launched more than a month ago by the internationally recognised government, to take control of territory from Houthi fighters.
In a separate statement, government forces spokesman, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the army had carried out 875 attacks on Houthi positions on Saturday, “neutralising” about 130 Houthi commanders and fighters and destroying or disabling 50 vehicles and missile launchers.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.
‘Two narratives’
Also on Saturday, a series of strikes killed at least 27 people and wounded about 30 others in Sanaa province, the Houthi-run ⁠Saba news ⁠agency reported.

Handout picture released by Paraguay's Attorney General's Office shows impeached Paraguay's President Santiago Pena, left, arriving at the Attorney General's Office in Asuncion on November 7, 2026 [AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and The Associated PressPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been charged after spending the morning at the attorney general’s office in Asunción for questioning, a day after being impeached over his alleged involvement in a banking scandal that has left nearly half the country unable to access their savings.
The former president, who was placed under house arrest on Friday, was charged over the scandal. The Reuters news agnecy reported that Pena was charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain.

The scandal centres on Pena’s ties to Ueno, a digital bank that grew rapidly during his presidency, partly through an injection of more than $800m in public funds, and attracted millions of customers.
The bank’s collapse has prompted days of protests across Paraguay, with thousands taking to the streets demanding access to their savings. Some demonstrations have turned violent, with protesters clashing with police.
Pena, who held a stake in Ueno’s parent company until March 2025, has denied wrongdoing, arguing that the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter.

Pope Leo XIV waves to the faithful upon his arrival at Paris London Park to lead a mass, in Paysandu, western Uruguay, 7 November 2026 [Daniel Dal Zennaro/EPA]By AFP, AP and ReutersPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Pope Leo XIV has addressed tens of thousands of people who gathered for his first mass in western Uruguay as he continues his 12-day tour of Latin America.
The head of the Roman Catholic Church urged the crowd at Paris London Park in Paysandu on Saturday to be “bridge builders” and “share the joy” of their faith.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to vote in US general electionlist 2 of 3Pope Leo XIV arrives in Uruguay starting 12-day Latin America tourlist 3 of 3Pope Leo XIV arrives for South American tour after cancer surgeryend of list
More than 30,000 people – many from Uruguay but also from neighbouring Argentina and Brazil – had registered in advance to attend the service, about 375km (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said another 10,000 had shown up beyond that, despite the morning rain and blustery, grey skies.
It was the first mass of Leo’s three-nation South American tour – which also includes Argentina and Peru – which had been in doubt after the 71-year-old American pope underwent lung cancer surgery last month.
The pontiff appeared to be in good health on Saturday. While flying from Rome to Montevideo, Leo told reporters his speedy recovery was due to “trusting God, good doctors, good surgeons, and overall, I think a healthy lifestyle”.
His visit to Latin America comes as the region contends with sharp political divisions, with several right-wing leaders coming to power since United States President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January last yea...
